items.title: Hinton Milt — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: At the same time Ben Burney was at the College Inn.

ctx.x: And who worked there… I‟m sure that was 1932, and we go to work at a place owned by Al Capone. I never will forget it. A guy named Andy Packard was his lieutenant. A small club, not much bigger then this room around here. It seated about 60 people but the news got around that Eddie was playing there and all these gangsters came in, select people came to hear him. At the same time Ben Burney was at the College Inn. He was a big bandleader and his musical arranger and conductor was a guy named Dexter Deal. Dexter…
But he played saxophone didn‟t he?

items.title: Milt Hinton interviewed by Joe Williams, Majesty of the Seas, May 31, 1995
items.q: Dix Debill was the conductor for Ben Bernie’s band.

ctx.x: He’d mention things about Jimmy Noone. And I remember because in the 30s I remember I was working with Eddie South, a great violin player, and I got the job to play with Eddie and he had just come back from Europe. And we got to give the men or what we call on the other side the gangsters a lot of credit for helping music along, because they almost closed and they kept music. Capone’s. Al Capone had the Cotton Club on Cicero. And he had people, he opened the Cotton Club with black entertainers and white…

Rubaiyat, for his gangster pals just to have some place to come and bring their ladies to have lunch. It seated like 75 or 100 people. He put Eddie South in there. And we played all these different places for him. And I remember, Dix Debill was the conductor for Ben Bernie’s band. And his father was a violin player. So he used to bring his father over to hear Eddie South. And Ben Pollock was playing a club in Chicago. And Jack Teagarden, Benny Goodman —
Woody Herman, all that bunch came out through Ben Pollock.
